items.title: Unit 1 Encounter the Phenomenon: "How can we model the motion of a delivery drone?" and "What does a graph show about a bike race?"

body.html: A prompt to ask questions and to say how the idea of modeling motion applies to a drone delivering a package and to a bike race. No data are given.

A model replaces a real, complicated situation with a simpler one (points, arrows, tables, graphs, equations) that keeps only the features that matter. Here we model the drone and each cyclist as a single point moving along one line, and describe them with positions, times, and velocities.

A graph of position against time for a bike race tells us where each cyclist is at every moment. A steeper line means a faster cyclist, a line that crosses another means one cyclist passes the other, and a flat line means the cyclist has stopped.

answer.html: We can model the drone's flight and the race with motion diagrams, tables, graphs, and equations; the same tools work for both. Sample questions for the board: How can a graph show who is leading the race at any moment? How does the drone's path look on a motion diagram when it speeds up or slows down?

check.html: The answer uses only ideas that this module develops (motion diagrams, position-time graphs, slope).

items.title: Module 2 Encounter the Phenomenon / CER / Revisit the Phenomenon: "How does a ship's sonar know how deep the water is?"

body.html: Make a claim, collect evidence, and give reasoning for how a sonar unit finds the depth of the water. As numbers for the evidence: a sound pulse is sent straight down and its echo returns after 0.80 s; sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water.
Distance traveled by a signal moving at constant speed is speed multiplied by a time interval, 𝛥𝑥= ¯𝑣𝛥𝑡. The pulse travels down and back, so the depth is half of the total distance.

A sonar unit finds the depth by timing how long a sound pulse takes to go down to the bottom and return. Evidence from this module: Time interval is a difference of clock readings, 𝛥𝑡= 𝑡<sub>f</sub> −𝑡<sub>i</sub> (Lesson 3). Velocity is ¯𝑣= 𝛥𝑥/ 𝛥𝑡, so 𝛥𝑥= ¯𝑣𝛥𝑡 (Lesson 4). The total distance for the round trip is
The pulse goes down and back up, so the one-way distance (the depth) is half of the total:

answer.html: A sonar unit knows the depth by measuring the echo's round-trip time and using distance = speed × time interval, then halving it for the one-way trip. Here the depth is 6.0 × 10<sup>2</sup> m (600 m).

check.html: A timing error of 1 ms changes the depth by <sup>(1500)(0.001)</sup>
= 0.75 m, which is why the unit needs an accurate timer.

items.title: Lesson 1 Focus Question: How can you tell that a boat on a lake is moving?

body.html: Motion is a change in position over time, measured relative to something that is treated as fixed.

answer.html: You know the boat is moving when its position changes relative to a reference such as the dock, a buoy, or the shoreline, which stay in place.

check.html: If the boat stays at the same distance from the buoy as time passes, it is at rest relative to the buoy.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Figure 1): A long-exposure photograph of a cyclist riding past a row of parked bicycles shows the moving cyclist blurry and the parked bicycles sharp. How would the picture differ if the cyclist had stopped?

body.html: The blur comes from the cyclist's position changing while the shutter was open.

answer.html: The cyclist would be sharp (not blurry), just like the parked bicycles.

check.html: An object at rest does not change position during the exposure.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It?: Identify the two pieces of information you need at each observation to describe a skater gliding along a straight line.

answer.html: The skater's position (where she is on the line) and the time of the observation (when she is there).

check.html: Describing straight-line motion means giving place and time together.

items.title: Lesson 1, Particle model (Figure 3): A particle-model diagram of a skateboarder shows 6 dots, each 0.80 m from the next, taken every 0.50 s. Explain how it shows that the skateboarder's speed is not changing, and find the speed.

body.html: Spacing = 0.80 m per interval, interval = 0.50 s.
In a motion diagram the images are taken at equal time intervals, so the spacing between dots shows how far the object moved in each interval.

answer.html: The dots are evenly spaced, so the skateboarder moves the same distance in each equal time interval; the speed is constant at 1.6 m/s.

check.html: If the dots got closer together or farther apart, the speed would be changing.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It?: Describe how you would model the motion of a skier going straight down a ski slope.

body.html: Use the particle model: the skier's size is small compared with the length of the slope.

answer.html: Replace the skier with a single dot at a central point of the body (such as the hips) and plot a dot at the skier's position at equal time intervals. If the dots spread farther apart down the slope, the skier is speeding up; if they stay evenly spaced, the speed is constant.

check.html: The model ignores arm, pole, and ski movement, as the particle model should.

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress, Problem 1: A classmate says a motion diagram is like a video of the object. Explain what a motion diagram really shows and what the spacing between dots tells you.

answer.html: A motion diagram is a set of dots showing an object's position at successive, equal time intervals, not a continuous video. The dots show where the object was at each time, and the spacing tells how fast it moved: closely spaced dots mean slow motion and widely spaced dots mean fast motion.

check.html: Equal time between dots is what lets spacing stand for speed.

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress, Problem 2: Draw a particle-model motion diagram for a jogger moving at a steady pace along a straight path. Show 6 dots.

body.html: A steady pace means equal distances in equal time intervals, so the dots are evenly spaced.
Choose one point on the jogger, such as the waist, and mark its position at equal time intervals.

answer.html: A straight row of six equally spaced dots, as drawn. I used a point at the jogger's waist.

check.html: Equal spacing means constant speed.

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress, Problem 3: A bus approaches a bus stop, covering 8 m, 6 m, 4 m, and 2 m in four successive 1.0 s intervals, moving left to right, and stops. Draw its particle-model motion diagram and say what point on the bus you used.

body.html: The distances in successive intervals decrease: 8, 6, 4, 2 m. The dots are therefore at 0, 8, 14, 18, and 20 m.
Smaller spacing in equal time intervals means the bus is slowing down.

answer.html: Five dots moving left to right with the spacing shrinking from 8 m to 6 m to 4 m to 2 m, and the last dot at the bus stop. I used a point at the center of the bus body, though any single fixed point on the bus works.

check.html: The spacing decreases as the bus stops, and the total distance is 8 + 6 + 4 + 2 = 20 m.

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress, Problem 4: Draw a particle model for a drone flying right to left at a constant speed. Show five dots. What point on the drone did you choose?

body.html: The drone moves right to left and the four intervals between images are equal.
Equal spacing means a constant speed.

answer.html: Five evenly spaced dots (four equal intervals) in a row, with the motion pointing right to left. I chose the center of the drone's body, ignoring the spinning propellers.

check.html: The center of the body is a good point because it does not move relative to the rest of the drone.

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress, Problem 5: Critical Thinking, two cyclists start together; the first crosses the finish line when the second is two-thirds of the way there. Draw motion diagrams for both.

body.html: In the same time the first cyclist covers the whole distance and the second covers <sup>2</sup> <sub>3</sub> of it, so the second cyclist's spacing is <sup>2</sup> <sub>3</sub> as large.

Use four equal time intervals. If cyclist 1 moves 1.5 units per interval, the finish is 6 units away. Cyclist 2 moves <sup>2</sup> <sub>3</sub>(1.5) = 1.0 unit per interval and reaches 4 units when cyclist 1 is at 6.

answer.html: Two rows of dots from the same start. Cyclist 1's dots are spaced farther apart (1.5 units). When cyclist 1's last dot is on the finish line (6 units), cyclist 2's last dot is at 4 units, two-thirds of the way.

check.html: Both rows have the same number of dots (same time), but cyclist 2's dots are closer together, which means slower.

items.title: Review the News (sample): Search for a news story about how sports teams use motion capture. A

question.html: sample summary: cameras track reflective dots on an athlete's joints at equal time intervals, and software turns the dot positions into a particle-style model used to compare techniques.

answer.html: Dots that get closer together mean the car is slowing; dots that get farther apart mean it is speeding up; evenly spaced dots mean constant speed. The news summary should name the technology, what is measured (positions at equal times), and one use.

check.html: Each statement about spacing matches the particle-model rule for equal time intervals.

items.title: Unit 1 Encounter the Phenomenon: "How can we model motion and forces?" and "What does the graph show about the race?"

body.html: A prompt to ask questions and to say how the idea of modeling motion applies. No data are given.

A model replaces a real, complicated situation with a simpler one (points, arrows, graphs, equations) that keeps only the features that matter. In this unit we model an object as a single point (particle model) moving along one line, and describe it with positions, times, and velocities.
A graph of position against time for a race tells us where each racer is at every moment. A steeper line means a faster racer, and where two lines cross the racers are side by side.

answer.html: We can model motion with diagrams, tables, graphs, and equations, and forces will be added as the cause of changes in that motion. Sample questions for the board: How does the slope of a position-time graph tell who is winning? How do forces change a motion graph?

check.html: The answer uses only ideas that this module develops (motion diagrams, position-time graphs, slope).

items.title: Module 2 Encounter the Phenomenon / CER / Revisit the Phenomenon: "How does a GPS unit know where you are?"

body.html: Make a claim, collect evidence, and give reasoning for how a GPS unit knows your position.

A position is a vector measured from an origin of a coordinate system. A GPS receiver must therefore (1) use a coordinate system with an agreed origin, and (2) measure times accurately, because distance traveled by a signal is speed multiplied by a time interval, 𝛥𝑥= 𝑣𝛥𝑡.

A GPS unit finds its position in a coordinate system by timing signals from satellites whose positions are known. Evidence from this module: Position is the vector from the origin to an object (Lesson 2). Time intervals are differences of clock readings, 𝛥𝑡= 𝑡<sub>f</sub> −𝑡<sub>i</sub>. Velocity is ¯𝑣= 𝛥𝑥/ 𝛥𝑡, so 𝛥𝑥= ¯𝑣𝛥𝑡 (Lesson 4). Moving objects can be located with 𝑥= ¯𝑣𝑡+ 𝑥<sub>i</sub>.

A signal travels at a known, constant speed. If a satellite records when the signal left and the receiver records when it arrived, the distance equals speed times the time interval. Because a tiny timing error becomes a large distance error, the satellites carry very accurate atomic clocks (see Scientific Breakthroughs). Distances from several satellites with known positions fix the receiver's position, and repeating this as time passes gives velocity from 𝛥𝑥/ 𝛥𝑡.

answer.html: A GPS unit knows where you are by measuring signal travel times from satellites (distance = speed × time interval) and combining distances from satellites at known positions. This evidence supports the claim.

check.html: A timing error of 1 𝜇s at the speed of light gives roughly 300 m, which explains why accurate clocks matter.

items.title: Lesson 1 Focus Question: How do you know that something is moving?

body.html: Motion is a change in position over time, measured relative to something that is treated as fixed.

answer.html: You know an object is moving when its position changes relative to a reference such as the ground, tree, or camera, while the background stays put.

check.html: This matches Figure 2: the runner moves relative to the tree.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It? (Figure 1): How would the picture differ if the train were sitting still?

body.html: The blur in Figure 1 comes from the train's position changing while the shutter was open.

answer.html: The train would be sharp (not blurry), just like the hay bales.

check.html: An object at rest does not change position during the exposure.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It?: Identify two factors you must know to describe straight-line motion.

answer.html: Where the object is (its position) and when it is there (the time).

check.html: The book states that motion is a description of place and time.

items.title: Lesson 1, Particle model (Figure 3): Explain how the particle model shows the runner's speed is not changing.

body.html: In a motion diagram the images are taken at equal time intervals, so the spacing between dots shows how far the object moved in each interval.

answer.html: The dots are evenly spaced. The runner moves the same distance in each equal time interval, so her speed is constant.

check.html: If the dots got closer or farther apart, the speed would be changing.

items.title: Lesson 1, Get It?: Describe how you would model the motion of the hiker at the beginning of the module.

body.html: Use the particle model: the hiker's size is small compared with the distance traveled.

answer.html: Replace the hiker with a single dot at a central point of the body (such as the waist) and plot a dot at the hiker's position at equal time intervals. Evenly spaced dots mean constant speed.

check.html: The model ignores arm and leg movement, as the particle model should.

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress, Problem 1: How does a motion diagram represent an object's motion?

answer.html: A motion diagram shows an object's position at successive, equal time intervals. The dots show where the object was at each time, and the spacing between dots shows how fast it moved (close dots mean slow, far-apart dots mean fast).

check.html: Matches the Study Guide summary for Lesson 1.

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress, Problem 2: Particle model motion diagram for a bike rider moving at a constant pace along a straight path.

body.html: Constant pace means equal distances in equal time intervals, so the dots are evenly spaced.
Choose one point on the rider and bike, such as the center of the wheel hub, and mark its position at equal time intervals.

answer.html: A straight row of equally spaced dots, as drawn.

check.html: Equal spacing means constant speed.

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress, Problem 3: Particle motion diagram for the car in Figure 4 stopping at a stop sign. What point on the car did you use?

body.html: In Figure 4 the car moves right to left. The distance traveled in each interval gets smaller: about 2 units, then about 1.5 units, then about 1 unit between the last images.
Smaller spacing in equal time intervals means the car is slowing down.

answer.html: Four dots (three intervals) moving right to left, with the spacing shrinking from about 2 units to 1.5 units to 1 unit and the last dot at the stop sign. I used a point at the center of the car (the middle of the body), though any single fixed point on the car works.

check.html: The spacing decreases as the car stops.

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress, Problem 4: Particle model for the bird in Figure 5. What point on the bird did you choose?

body.html: The bird flies left to right, and the three intervals between images are about the same length.
Equal spacing means a constant speed.

answer.html: Four evenly spaced dots (three equal intervals) moving left to right. I chose the center of the bird's body (the chest/torso), ignoring the flapping wings.

check.html: The torso is a better point than a wing tip because it does not move up and down relative to the body.

items.title: Lesson 1 Check Your Progress, Problem 5: Critical Thinking, two runners; the first crosses the finish line when the second is three-fourths of the way.

body.html: In the same time the first runner covers the whole distance and the second covers 3/4 of it, so the second runner's spacing is 3/4 as large.
Use equal time intervals. If runner 1 moves 1 unit per interval and the finish is 4 units away, then runner 2 moves 0.75 units per interval, reaching 3 units when runner 1 is at 4.

answer.html: Two rows of dots from the same start. Runner 1's dots are spaced farther apart. When runner 1's last dot is on the finish line, runner 2's last dot is at 3/4 of that distance.

check.html: Both rows have the same number of dots (same time), but runner 2's are closer together, which means slower.
